newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada Q1 earnings seen hurt by commodities.
newsitem.headline: Canada Q1 earnings seen hurt by commodities.

text.p: Lower commodity prices are expected to take their toll on Canadian resource companies in the first quarter, marring an otherwise rosy profit picture for corporate Canada.

Analysts said positive economic conditions and strong margins should fuel bottom-line growth when Canadian corporate earnings roll out over the next few weeks, with lagging resources expected to catch up in the second half of 1997.
"We're still looking at pretty solid profit growth this year, something in the order of 10 to 15 percent," said economist Doug Porter at brokerage Nesbitt Burns.

"If there is a concern, it's that a lot of the resource prices are still at a fairly low ebb, and so I'd say in general a lot of the export-oriented industries will face a bit of a struggle on the revenue side," he said.
Gold producers, whose profits were halved in the fourth quarter, were expected to be hit again as bullion continued to slide.

Dunnery Best, director of private client investing at Toronto-based brokerage Midland Walwyn, said he expected most gold producers in his survey of 30 senior and intermediate players to record losses.

"Sixty-five percent are going to report lower year-over-year quarterly earnings or larger losses. And over 60 percent are going to report losses in the first quarter compared to just 10 percent last year," said Best.

He said the sector's steep fixed costs made it especially vulnerable to nose-diving gold prices. The average spot price of bullion fell $49 an ounce to $351 in the first quarter of 1997 from the same quarter a year earlier.
But Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer and Co. in New York, said problems in the gold sector should be just about over.

"My feeling is that we're going to see the European Monetary Union enter a crisis phase in the next few weeks.... so I have a feeling we're going to see a big move up in gold in that period," Metz said.
Base metal miners and paper and forest companies were also expected to post a weak first quarter before an expected turnaround in commodity prices in the second half of 1997.
"I don't think you're going to see real strong numbers out of the resource stocks. The mines and the forests are all going to be looking fairly weak," Best said.
The energy sector, which bucked the resource slump in 1996, was expected to turn weaker this year.
"It's had quite a strong run recently but the more recent slippage in energy prices will hurt a little," said Porter.
But soft earnings by export-oriented companies should be outweighed by continued growth at home, with banks, industrials and consumer products all facing a profitable quarter.
"I think a lot of the sectors that are geared to domestic spending should begin to see some real benefits from the improving economy," Porter said.

He said banks had probably seen their biggest profit gains -- Canada's big six banks earned C$6 billion ($4.4 billion) last year, capping three years of record earnings -- but that there was plenty of room for moderate growth.

"The small backup we're beginning to see in mortgage rates suggests that perhaps the ideal conditions of the second half of 1996 are now behind us, but that doesn't mean that profits can't grow a little more," Porter said.
"Most factors are working highly in favor of financial services right now, still low interest rates, low inflation, an improving economy, an improving credit growth," he said.
Best said a strong U.S. economy would also buoy profits of Canadian export-oriented industrial companies.
